---
title: "Selection intensity versus diversity"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
```

Every cycle, a breeder decides how many lines to recycle as parents. Using
only the very best lines gives the most gain next cycle. It also narrows the
genetic base, and a narrow base has less variance to select on in the
cycles after that. This trade-off between short-term gain and long-term
potential has no single right answer. The best choice depends on your
horizon, and on how much diversity you are willing to spend.

This article measures the trade-off for a line pipeline and shows how a
Pareto front turns it into a menu of good options.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyagsim)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## The study

We use `line_pipeline()`, run for six cycles, and vary the number of parents
recycled from the advanced yield trial:

```{r}
pipeline <- line_pipeline(
  n_parents = tune(),
  n_crosses = 30, progeny_per_cross = 15, n_ayt = 80, cycles = 6,
  founders = asr_founders(n_chr = 10, seg_sites = 100)
)

metrics <- sim_metric_set(release_gain, genetic_variance, expected_heterozygosity, gain_per_year)

res <- tune_grid(
  pipeline,
  resamples = sim_replicates(15, seed = 1),
  grid = data.frame(n_parents = c(4, 8, 16, 32, 64)),
  metrics = metrics,
  control = control_sim(save_outcomes = TRUE)
)
```

## Gain over time

```{r, fig.alt = "Mean genetic value of the parents over six cycles for five numbers of parents. Few parents lead early; more parents catch up by the last cycles."}
traj <- collect_trajectories(res)
avg <- aggregate(cbind(mean, heterozygosity) ~ n_parents + year, data = traj, FUN = mean)

ggplot(avg, aes(year, mean, colour = factor(n_parents))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean genetic value of parents (founder SDs)", colour = "Parents",
       title = "Gain over six breeding cycles")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Expected heterozygosity of the parents over six cycles, falling fastest with few parents."}
ggplot(avg, aes(year, heterozygosity, colour = factor(n_parents))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Heterozygosity (fraction of founders')", colour = "Parents",
       title = "Diversity left in the parents")
```

Few parents spend diversity fast. Expected heterozygosity is the chance two
alleles drawn at random from the parents differ, and it falls each cycle in
proportion to how few parents there are. Within six cycles this already costs
gain. Four parents lead for the first three cycles, then 8 and 16 parents pass
them, and 16 finish highest. Sixty-four parents keep the most diversity but
select too weakly to keep up.

## The menu: a Pareto front

```{r}
collect_metrics(res, type = "wide")[, c("n_parents", "release_gain", "release_gain_se",
                                        "expected_heterozygosity", "genetic_variance")]
pareto_front(res, metrics = c("release_gain", "expected_heterozygosity"))
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Gain of released lines against remaining heterozygosity for each number of parents, with the Pareto front highlighted."}
autoplot(res, type = "pareto", metric = c("release_gain", "expected_heterozygosity"))
```

Every design on the front is a defensible choice. Moving along it trades gain
now for diversity later, at the exchange rate the plot shows. Designs off the
front can be dropped: some other design does at least as well on both goals.

## Choose with a diversity floor

If your program has a rule such as "keep at least 60% of the founders'
heterozygosity after six cycles", make it a constraint and let the helpers
pick the highest gain that respects it:

```{r}
show_best(res, metric = "release_gain", constraints = list(expected_heterozygosity = 0.6))
```

## Going further

* Run longer horizons (`cycles = 15`) to see the few-parent designs fall
  behind, as in [Why simulate?](why-simulate.html).
* Tune `n_parents` and `n_crosses` together with `tune_bayes()`, under a
  heterozygosity constraint.
* Replace truncation selection with optimal contribution selection inside an
  `alphasim_program()` of your own (for example with the optiSel package), and
  compare it with this pipeline in a `sim_set()`.
